title: Pains that God sends to heal
source_text: Εἰ δὲ τὰ καταχρηστικῶς οὕτως ὀνομαζόμενα, λεγόμενα σωματικὰ κακὰ καὶ ἐκτὸς, τίς φησι, δεδόσθω ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε τούτων τινὰ πεποιηκέναι τὸν θεὸν, ἵνα διὰ τούτων ἐπιστρέψῃ τινάς, καὶ τί ἄτοπον ὁ λόγος ἔχειν δύναται; ὥσπερ γὰρ, εἰ καταχρηστικῶς ἀκουόντων ἡμῶν κακὰ τοὺς προσαγομένους πόνους τοῖς παιδευομένοις ὑπὸ πατέρων καὶ διδασκάλων καὶ παιδαγωγῶν, ἢ ὑπὸ ἰατρῶν τοῖς θεραπείας ἕνεκεν τεμνομένοις ἢ καυτηριαζομένοις. λέγομεν τὸν πατέρα κακοποιεῖν τοῖς υἱοῖς ἢ τοὺς παιδαγωγοὺς ἢ τοὺς διδασκάλους ἢ τοὺς ἰατροὺς, οὐδὲν ἂν κατηγοροῖντο οἱ τύπτοντες ἢ οἱ τέμνοντες· οὕτως. εἰ ὁ θεὸς λέγεται τὰ τοιαδὶ ἐπάγειν ἐπιστροφῆς καὶ θεραπείας ἕνεκεν τῶν δεομένων τοιούτων πόνων, οὐδὲν ἂν ἄτοπον ὁ λόγος ἔχοι· οὔτ᾿ ἂν καταβαίνῃ „κακὰ παρὰ κυρίου ἐπὶ πύλας Ἱερουσαλὴμ,“ τὴν ὑπόστασιν ἔχοντα ἐν τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν πολεμίων πόνοις. προσαγομένοις αὐτοῖς εἰς ἐπιστροφὴν. οὔτ᾿ ἂν ἐπισκέπτηται „ἐν ῥάβδῳ τὰς ἀνομίας“ τῶν ἐγκαταλιπόντων „τὸν νόμον“ τοῦ θεοῦ „καὶ ἐν μάστιξι τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν,“ οὔτ᾿ ἂν λέγῃ τό· „ἔχεις ἄνθρακας πυρὸς, κάθισαι ἐπ᾿ αὐτοὺς, οὗτοι ἔσονταί σοι βοήθεια.“ τοῦτον δὲ τὸν τρόπον καὶ τὸ „ὁ ποιῶν εἰρήνην καὶ κτίζων κακὰ“ διηγούμεθα· κτίζει γὰρ τὰ σωματικὰ ἢ τὰ ἐκτὸς κακὰ, καθαίρων καὶ παιδεύων τοὺς μὴ βουληθέντας παιδευθῆναι λόγῳ καὶ διδασκαλίᾳ ὑγιεῖ. καὶ ταῦτα μὲν εἰς τὸ πῶς μὲν ὁ θεὸς κακὰ ἐποίει;
pass_a_gloss: But if the things so named by extension of usage (καταχρηστικῶς), called bodily (σωματικά) and external (ἐκτός) evils, someone says (τις φησί), let it be granted (δίδωμι, perf. imperative δεδόσθω) that God sometimes (ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε) has made some of these, so that through them he may turn back (ἐπιστρέφω) some people, and what absurdity (ἄτοπον) can the doctrine (λόγος) have? For just as, if we understanding by extension of usage as evils the pains (πόνοι) applied (προσάγω) to those being educated (παιδεύω) by fathers and teachers (διδάσκαλοι) and tutors (παιδαγωγοί), or by doctors (ἰατροί) to those being cut (τέμνω) or cauterized (καυτηριάζω) for the sake of treatment (θεραπεία), say that the father does evil (κακοποιέω) to his sons, or the tutors or the teachers or the doctors, those who strike (τύπτω) or cut would in no way be accused (κατηγορέω); so, if God is said to bring (ἐπάγω) such things for the sake of turning back (ἐπιστροφή) and healing of those needing such pains, the doctrine would have nothing absurd; nor if ‘evils come down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem,’ having their reality (ὑπόστασις) in the pains from the enemies (πολέμιοι) applied to them for turning back; nor if he visits (ἐπισκέπτομαι) ‘with a rod (ῥάβδος) the lawless deeds (ἀνομίαι)’ of those who have forsaken (ἐγκαταλείπω) ‘the law (νόμος)’ of God ‘and with scourges (μάστιγες) their sins (ἁμαρτίαι)’; nor if he says: ‘You have coals of fire (ἄνθρακες πυρός); sit upon them; these will be a help (βοήθεια) to you.’ In this manner we also explain (διηγέομαι) ‘the one making peace and creating evils’: for he creates the bodily or external evils, purifying (καθαίρω) and training (παιδεύω) those who were not willing (βούλομαι) to be trained by word (λόγος) and sound (ὑγιής) teaching (διδασκαλία). And these things [are said] in reply to ‘how did God make evils?’
pass_b_english: But if someone means the things loosely so called, the so-called bodily and external evils, let it be granted that God has at times made some of these, in order to turn certain people back through them; what absurdity can the doctrine then contain? For suppose we loosely take as evils the pains that fathers, teachers and tutors inflict on those they are training, or that doctors inflict on those they cut or cauterize for the sake of treatment, and say that the father does evil to his sons, or that tutors, teachers or doctors do so: those who strike or cut would face no accusation at all. In the same way, if God is said to bring such things for the sake of the conversion and healing of those who need such pains, the doctrine would contain nothing absurd.

Nor would it be absurd if “evils come down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem” (Micah 1:12), evils that consisted in the pains inflicted by enemies and brought upon them for their conversion; nor if he visits “with a rod the iniquities” of those who have forsaken “the law” of God, “and with scourges their sins” (Psalm 89:30–32); nor if he says: “You have coals of fire; sit upon them; these will be a help to you” (Isaiah 47:14–15).

In this way we also explain “who makes peace and creates evils” (Isaiah 45:7): he creates bodily or external evils, purifying and training those who were unwilling to be trained by word and sound teaching. So much, then, for “How did God make evils?”

choices.choice: τίς φησι in the opening sentence is doubtful; read as enclitic τις φησί (‘if someone means’) and folded into the condition. The Perseus punctuation of this chapter has stray full stops inside sentences (after καυτηριαζομένοις, οὕτως and πόνοις); the English follows the obvious syntax across them. ‘Does evil to his sons’ keeps the link between κακοποιεῖν and κακά. Micah 1:12 LXX as in section 55 (Origen’s subjunctive καταβαίνῃ). LXX renumbering: ‘visit with a rod their iniquities and with scourges their sins’ is LXX Psalm 88:33, with ‘forsake my law’ from 88:31 = English Psalm 89:30–32; Origen recasts it in the third person (‘the law of God’). Isaiah 47:14–15 LXX: ἔχεις ἄνθρακας πυρός, κάθισαι ἐπ᾿ αὐτούς· οὗτοι ἔσονταί σοι βοήθεια; the LXX differs here from the Hebrew, which denies that the coals give warmth, and Origen reads the LXX as healing punishment. ‘Sound teaching’ (διδασκαλίᾳ ὑγιεῖ) may echo the Pastoral Letters’ phrase (1 Timothy 1:10; Titus 1:9), not cited inline because it is a common expression rather than a clear allusion.
‘if “evils came down”’ → ‘if “evils come down”’ (Origen changes the LXX κατέβη to the subjunctive καταβαίνῃ)
kept the doubtful τίς φησι as ‘if someone means’ (already noted)
Micah 1:12, Psalm 89:30–32 (LXX 88:31–33), Isaiah 47:14–15 and Isaiah 45:7 checked against the LXX; numbering correct
